title: Three hundred years of the Guru Granth
hookLine: Sikhs mark three centuries since the Granth became Guru
tomorrow: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak

cards: Each morning in a gurdwara, someone opens the Guru Granth Sahib at random and reads the first hymn on the left-hand page aloud. That reading is the hukamnama, the order of the day. Nobody chooses it; it's received.
Sikhs don't treat this as reading a book. They treat it as listening to the Guru. So where did a book get the authority of a living teacher?
The answer goes back to a riverbank far to the south of Punjab, at Nanded, and to the last days of the tenth Guru. Today: three hundred years of the Guru Granth.

teach.h: WHO COMES AFTER THE TENTH GURU?
teach.b: First, who comes next. For generations, each Guru had named a successor, a living person. Guru Gobind Singh's own sons had all died before him, as this path told in its harder days.

Second, the answer at Nanded. Tradition says that there, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh placed the Granth on the seat of the Guru and bowed before it. There would be no human Guru after him.

The Word itself would be the Guru, and the Khalsa, the community, would carry on its guidance together. Third, the words people still sing. In gurdwaras, after the Ardas, a couplet from the later tradition is sung.
Its sense: by the order of the Timeless One the Panth was founded, and every Sikh is commanded to accept the Granth as Guru.

teach.h: THE GRANTH ON THE GURU'S SEAT.
teach.b: Sikhs name the seat itself gur gaddi, the Guru's throne, and speak of the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru. Fourth, what it changed.
A living Guru can die, be captured, or face rival claimants.

teach.h: THE SAME GURU IN EVERY GURDWARA.
teach.b: A Guru who is the Word is the same wherever it is opened: every gurdwara holds the same Guru, in the same words, on the same raised seat under a canopy.
When Sikhs marked three centuries since Nanded, they gathered at Hazur Sahib, the gurdwara there, and in their own gurdwaras, to honor not a person but the Word.

how: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib on entering a gurdwara, read a hukamnama from it each morning, and after the Ardas sangats sing the couplet that commands Sikhs to accept the Granth as Guru.

games.q: you're Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded, near the end of your life, with no living sons. who will be Guru after you?
games.why: tradition says he placed the Granth on the Guru's seat and bowed to it, so the Word became the eternal Guru.

practice: If you're near the Guru Granth Sahib, you can bow before it, as Sikhs do when they enter; if not, lower your head a little, slowly, toward whatever you hold as wise: a sacred book, a teacher's words, or simply the quiet.
Stay low for a few breaths and notice what it feels like to put something above yourself on purpose. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow.

wordCard.voice: Gur gaddi. The Guru's seat, where, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh placed the Granth at Nanded, and the Word became the eternal Guru. Today's word.
